questions.q: Why does Harlow Creek Logistics end up with eight subscriptions instead of four?
options: Azure requires exactly two subscriptions per team regardless of design
One subscription per product team per environment, plus three platform subscriptions split by function, follows blast radius rather than the org chart
Each engineer needs a personal subscription
Eight is simply the Azure default subscription limit
questions.explain: Splitting prod from non-prod per team, plus connectivity/identity/management for Platform, means a mistake in one subscription can't spread into another team's or environment's resources.

questions.q: What specifically forces a spoke VNet's traffic to actually pass through the hub firewall, rather than just looking that way on a diagram?
options: A user-defined route (UDR) on the spoke subnet sending 0.0.0.0/0 to the firewall's private IP
VNet peering alone, with no additional configuration
Naming the spoke VNet with a 'spoke-' prefix
Assigning the spoke to the same resource group as the hub
questions.explain: Peering connects the networks, but without the UDR a VM would route to the internet directly, bypassing the firewall entirely.

questions.q: Why is the allowed-locations policy assigned at mg-hcl instead of at mg-landing-zones like the other three guardrails?
options: Because mg-hcl is a smaller management group than mg-landing-zones
It makes no difference which management group it's assigned to
Because Azure Policy cannot be assigned above the landing zones level
So that it also constrains Platform's own subscriptions, not just the product teams'
questions.explain: Assigning it one level higher binds sub-connectivity, sub-identity, and sub-management too -- a guardrail that exempts the team writing it isn't real enterprise governance.

questions.q: What does the hub VNet in this design actually contain?
options: Each product team's full application stack
Nothing; the hub is a placeholder with no resources
Only shared services: the Azure Firewall subnet, the gateway subnet, and shared services like DNS -- never a team's own workload
A copy of every spoke VNet's subnets
questions.explain: The hub holds only shared infrastructure that every spoke depends on; actual application workloads live in the spoke VNets.

questions.q: Why do spoke VNets peer only to the hub and never to each other?
options: Spoke-to-spoke peering is technically impossible in Azure
Because each spoke uses a different cloud provider
To reduce the total number of VNets in the subscription
So that cross-team traffic passes through the hub firewall, where it can be inspected and logged, instead of flowing unmonitored
questions.explain: Routing all inter-team traffic through the hub keeps the firewall as the one place that inspection and logging actually happen.
